title: Customer Credit Risk
answer: Customer credit risk is the chance that a business customer will not pay an invoice on the agreed terms, which makes it a core concern for accounts receivable and a secondary concern for payables when a company's own suppliers face the same question. The work covers setting credit limits and payment terms, monitoring aging balances, deciding when to hold orders, chasing overdue invoices, and estimating bad debt provisions. It also touches trade credit insurance, credit reference reports, and the cash flow forecasts that depend on expected collections. crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Customer credit risk is the chance that a business customer will not pay an invoice on the agreed terms, which makes it a core concern for accounts receivable and a secondary concern for payables when a company's own suppliers face the same question. The work covers setting credit limits and payment terms, monitoring aging balances, deciding when to hold orders, chasing overdue invoices, and estimating bad debt provisions. It also touches trade credit insurance, credit reference reports, and the cash flow forecasts that depend on expected collections. In the AI Accountant, this topic sits inside payables and receivables because the same customer data drives both the money owed to you and the money you owe.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The data usually comes from an ERP or accounting system, which holds invoices, payments, credit notes, and aging reports, plus external credit bureau files, financial statements, bank and trade references, and sometimes news or court records. Teams run this on spreadsheets, on credit management modules inside ERP suites, or on a data warehouse that feeds a scoring service. Machine learning models typically run in the cloud or on a company server, with a job that refreshes scores nightly or in real time as new invoices and payments arrive. The output lands back in the ERP as a credit limit, a risk score, or a collections work queue.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Analysts and models start by defining default, for example an invoice more than a set number of days past due, and then assemble features such as payment history, days beyond terms, order size, industry, and macroeconomic indicators. Traditional scorecards use logistic regression or decision trees, while newer approaches use gradient boosting or neural networks on the same tabular data, sometimes adding text from emails or news. The model is trained on historical invoices, validated on a holdout period, and monitored for drift as customer behaviour changes. A credit committee or a senior analyst usually reviews large limits, unusual customers, and overrides, because a model score is an input rather than a final answer. Collections teams then use the score to prioritise calls, dunning letters, and payment plans.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Customer credit risk touches personal and business data, so provenance matters: credit bureau files, bank references, and internal payment records each carry different rights and accuracy obligations. In many jurisdictions, data protection rules give a customer the right to know what data is used and to correct errors, and contract terms govern how credit limits can be changed. Model risk management asks for documentation, validation, and an audit trail, especially when a score leads to a refused order or a withdrawn credit line. Bias and discrimination are live concerns even in business credit, because a model can learn from historical lending patterns that excluded certain regions or sectors. In practice, firms keep human review for adverse decisions, log every override, and document the main drivers of a score.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward continuous credit monitoring rather than annual reviews, with scores that update as payments arrive and as external data changes. More decisions will be embedded in the order to cash workflow, so a credit check happens at quote or order entry without a separate queue. Alternative data, such as open banking feeds and supply chain payment records, will supplement bureau files, though provenance and consent will remain the limiting factors. Generative and agentic tools may draft collection emails, summarise customer financials, and suggest payment plans, but the credit decision itself will still need a clear owner. The likely result is fewer manual credit reviews for small customers and more analyst time spent on large, complex, or disputed accounts.
